title: Family Routines and Rituals
text:
Family dinners, bedtime stories, Sunday visits to grandparents, the way a birthday is always celebrated: such habits seem too ordinary to study. In 2002, the psychologist Barbara Fiese, then at Syracuse University, and her colleagues set out to review what fifty years of research had found about them.

They drew a useful distinction. Routines are the practical, repeated tasks that keep a household running, such as who makes dinner and when children go to bed. They involve instrumental communication ("this is what needs to be done") and take little thought once established. Rituals are different. They carry symbolic meaning, say "this is who we are," and are often anticipated with pleasure and remembered long after. A routine dinner can become a ritual when it is a time the family reliably gathers and talks.

Across the studies they reviewed, regular routines and meaningful rituals were associated with a range of good outcomes: more competent parenting, better child health, including better management of chronic illnesses such as asthma, stronger academic achievement, and greater satisfaction in marriages. Disrupted routines, by contrast, often accompanied family stress.

The review helped bring attention to the quiet, repeated structure of family life as a source of stability.
lesson: Small repeated rituals, like a shared meal or a bedtime story, give a family structure and meaning. Protect a few of them even in busy seasons.
people: Barbara Fiese, Thomas Tomcho and colleagues
source: Fiese, B. H., Tomcho, T. J., Douglas, M., Josephs, K., Poltrock, S., and Baker, T. (2002). A review of 50 years of research on naturally occurring family routines and rituals: Cause for celebration? Journal of Family Psychology, 16(4), 381-390.
caveat: Most studies reviewed were correlational, so families that are already doing well may simply find it easier to keep routines.
